title: Business Intelligence
summary: Learn how companies turn raw data into trusted dashboards: KPIs, ETL/ELT, star schemas, OLAP, SQL, BI tools and governance, with hands-on Python and SQLite exercises.

lessons.title: What is business intelligence?
lessons.summary: Learn what BI is, who uses it, and how data flows from systems to decisions.

slides.title: Business intelligence
slides.text:
**BI** = the processes, technology and skills that turn business data into **reliable information** for decisions.

Reports, dashboards, metrics, self-service analysis.
slides.narration: Business intelligence, or BI, is the combination of processes, technology and skills that turns a company's data into reliable information for decisions. Its most visible products are reports and dashboards, but the real value is a shared, trusted view of the business.

slides.title: Who uses BI?
slides.text:
- **Executives:** company KPIs
- **Managers:** team performance
- **Analysts:** deeper questions
- **Operations:** daily monitoring (stock, tickets)
slides.narration: Everyone uses BI differently. Executives watch a handful of company-wide indicators, managers track their teams, analysts dig deeper with ad hoc questions, and operations teams monitor things like stock levels or support tickets every day.

slides.title: The BI stack
slides.text: Sources -> **ETL/ELT** -> **Data warehouse** -> **Semantic layer / models** -> **Dashboards & reports**
slides.narration: A typical BI stack moves data from source systems through pipelines, called ETL or ELT, into a central data warehouse. A semantic layer defines metrics consistently, and dashboards and reports sit on top for people to use.

slides.title: BI vs data analytics vs data science
slides.text:
- **BI:** what happened, monitored reliably (mostly descriptive)
- **Analytics:** why, ad hoc deep dives
- **Data science:** predictions, models

They overlap and share data.
slides.narration: BI focuses on reliable, repeatable reporting of what happened. Data analytics digs into why. Data science builds predictive models. The lines blur, and all three depend on the same clean, well-governed data.

slides.title: Single source of truth
slides.text:
Two reports, two different revenue numbers = **lost trust**.

BI aims for one agreed definition per metric.
slides.narration: A core goal of BI is a single source of truth. If sales and finance show different revenue numbers, people stop trusting data and go back to gut feeling. Agreed definitions and central data fix that.

lessons.notes:
## Definition

**Business intelligence (BI)** collects, integrates, models and presents business data so people can monitor performance and make decisions. It is mostly **descriptive and diagnostic**: what happened, where, and why.

## Typical BI questions

- How much revenue did we make this month, by product and region?
- Are we on track against target?
- Which customers are at risk of leaving?
- How long do support tickets take to resolve?

## The BI architecture

1. **Source systems:** ERP (finance, orders), CRM (customers), web analytics, spreadsheets, SaaS apps.
2. **Integration:** ETL or ELT pipelines extract, clean and load data.
3. **Storage:** a **data warehouse** or **lakehouse** (Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks, Amazon Redshift, Microsoft Fabric).
4. **Modeling and semantic layer:** star schemas and shared metric definitions.
5. **Presentation:** dashboards, reports, alerts, embedded analytics.
6. **Governance:** ownership, security, quality, documentation across all layers.

## BI roles

| Role | Focus |
|---|---|
| Data engineer | pipelines, warehouse |
| Analytics engineer | data models, tests, metric definitions (often with dbt) |
| BI developer / analyst | dashboards, reports, analysis |
| Business users | consume and explore |

## Value of BI

- Faster decisions, less time collecting numbers by hand.
- One agreed version of key metrics.
- Early warnings (alerts when a KPI drops).
- Self-service exploration for non-technical staff.

## BI in 2026

Cloud warehouses, semantic layers, and **AI assistants** that answer questions in natural language on top of governed data are standard features of major BI tools. They only work well when the underlying data and metric definitions are clean, which is what the rest of this course is about.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of BI?
options: Turning business data into reliable information for decisions
quiz.explain: BI supports decisions with trusted data.

quiz.q: Where does a BI stack usually store integrated data?
options: In a data warehouse or lakehouse
quiz.explain: A central warehouse integrates sources.

quiz.q: What does "single source of truth" mean?
options: Only one person can see data
One agreed, trusted definition and value for each metric
quiz.explain: Consistent definitions build trust.

lessons.task:
Pick a business you know (a café, an online shop, a gym).

1. List four decisions its managers make every week.
2. For each decision, name one number (metric) that would help.
3. Name the **source system** where that data lives today (cash register, booking app, spreadsheet...).
4. Draw the flow from those sources to a simple dashboard.

lessons.title: KPIs and metrics
lessons.summary: Define useful metrics and KPIs, compute growth and target attainment, and avoid vanity metrics.

slides.title: Metric vs KPI
slides.text:
- **Metric:** any measured number (page views, orders)
- **KPI** (key performance indicator): a metric tied to a **goal** and watched by leadership

All KPIs are metrics; few metrics are KPIs.
slides.narration: A metric is any number you measure. A key performance indicator is a metric directly tied to an important goal and watched closely by decision makers. Every KPI is a metric, but only a few metrics deserve to be KPIs.

slides.title: Good KPIs are...
slides.text:
- **Clearly defined** (formula, filters, time zone)
- **Actionable:** someone can move it
- Tied to a **target**
- **Owned** by a person
- Balanced: leading + lagging
slides.narration: Good KPIs have a precise definition, are actionable, have a target and an owner, and balance lagging indicators like revenue with leading indicators like sales pipeline that predict the future.

slides.title: Growth and attainment
slides.text:
**Growth %** = (current - previous) / previous x 100

**Target attainment %** = actual / target x 100
slides.code:
prev, curr, target = 80_000, 92_000, 100_000
growth = (curr - prev) / prev * 100
attain = curr / target * 100
print(f"{growth:+.1f}%  {attain:.1f}% of target")
# +15.0%  92.0% of target
slides.narration: Two calculations appear in almost every dashboard. Growth compares the current period with the previous one. Target attainment compares the actual value with the goal.

slides.title: Common business KPIs
slides.text:
- Revenue, gross margin %
- Customer acquisition cost (**CAC**)
- Customer lifetime value (**LTV**)
- Churn rate, retention
- Conversion rate, average order value
- MRR / ARR for subscriptions
slides.narration: Common KPIs include revenue and gross margin, the cost to acquire a customer, customer lifetime value, churn and retention, conversion rate, average order value, and for subscription businesses monthly and annual recurring revenue.

slides.title: Vanity metrics and Goodhart's law
slides.text:
- **Vanity:** big numbers that do not guide action (total sign-ups ever)
- **Goodhart's law:** "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure."
- Pair metrics: speed + quality
slides.narration: Beware vanity metrics, impressive numbers like total sign-ups ever that never go down and guide no decisions. And remember Goodhart's law: once a measure becomes a target, people game it. Pair metrics, such as ticket speed with customer satisfaction, to keep them honest.

lessons.notes:
## Metrics and KPIs

- **Metric:** a quantified measurement (orders per day).
- **KPI:** a metric that tracks progress toward a strategic goal, with a target and an owner.
- **North star metric:** the single metric that best captures customer value (e.g. weekly active teams).

## Defining a KPI precisely

Write a **metric definition**:

| Field | Example |
|---|---|
| Name | Monthly revenue |
| Formula | sum(order_amount) of completed orders, minus refunds |
| Grain | per calendar month, UTC |
| Filters | excludes test accounts and internal orders |
| Owner | Head of Sales |
| Target | 100,000 EUR per month |
| Source | warehouse table `fct_orders` |

## Core calculations

```python
prev, curr, target = 80000, 92000, 100000
growth = (curr - prev) / prev * 100          # +15.0 %
attainment = curr / target * 100             # 92.0 %
conversion = 230 / 11500 * 100               # orders / sessions = 2.0 %
churn = 45 / 1500 * 100                      # lost / customers at start = 3.0 %
aov = 92000 / 2300                           # average order value = 40.0
print(f'{growth:+.1f}% {attainment:.1f}% {conversion:.1f}% {churn:.1f}% {aov:.2f}')
```

Other important comparisons: **month over month (MoM)**, **year over year (YoY)** (removes seasonality), **year to date (YTD)**, and **CAGR** for multi-year growth.

## Leading vs lagging

- **Lagging:** results (revenue, churn). Accurate but late.
- **Leading:** predictors (pipeline value, trial sign-ups, NPS). Early but less certain.

## Frameworks

- **Balanced scorecard:** financial, customer, internal process, learning and growth.
- **OKRs:** Objectives with measurable Key Results.
- **SMART** targets.

## Pitfalls

- Vanity metrics (cumulative totals, raw page views).
- Ratios without the counts behind them.
- Changing definitions without versioning: annotate dashboards when a definition changes.
- **Goodhart's law:** pair metrics so improving one cannot hide damage to another.

quiz.q: Revenue went from 80,000 to 92,000. What is the growth?
Which is a leading indicator for future sales?
options: Value of the current sales pipeline
quiz.explain: Pipeline predicts future revenue.

quiz.q: What does Goodhart's law warn about?
options: A measure turned into a target can be gamed
quiz.explain: People optimize the number rather than the goal.

exercise.title: KPI scorecard
exercise.prompt:
Build a KPI scorecard.

Input: first line `n`, then `n` lines: `name previous current target` (numbers may have decimals; previous and target are not zero; higher values are better for every KPI).

For each KPI print:
```
name: growth +X.X% | target Y.Y% | STATUS
```
- growth = (current - previous) / previous x 100, with a sign and **1 decimal** (use the `+` format flag)
- target attainment = current / target x 100 with **1 decimal**
- STATUS is `on track` if attainment is at least 100, `close` if at least 90, otherwise `behind`
exercise.starter:
n = int(input())
for _ in range(n):
    name, prev, curr, target = input().split()
    prev, curr, target = float(prev), float(curr), float(target)
    # compute growth, attainment and status
exercise.solution:
n = int(input())
for _ in range(n):
    name, prev, curr, target = input().split()
    prev, curr, target = float(prev), float(curr), float(target)
    growth = (curr - prev) / prev * 100
    att = curr / target * 100
    status = 'on track' if att >= 100 else 'close' if att >= 90 else 'behind'
    print(f'{name}: growth {growth:+.1f}% | target {att:.1f}% | {status}')

tests.output:
orders: growth +25.0% | target 107.1% | on track
retention: growth +3.5% | target 97.8% | close
nps: growth -5.0% | target 76.0% | behind

signups: growth +0.0% | target 111.1% | on track
margin: growth +7.1% | target 90.0% | close

lessons.title: Data sources
lessons.summary: Map where business data lives: operational databases, SaaS apps, files, events and external data.

slides.title: Operational systems
slides.text:
- **ERP:** orders, invoices, inventory (SAP, Oracle, Dynamics, Odoo)
- **CRM:** leads, customers, deals (Salesforce, HubSpot)
- **E-commerce / POS:** sales transactions
- **HR, finance, support** tools
slides.narration: Most BI data starts in operational systems. ERPs handle orders, invoices and inventory. CRMs track leads and customers. Shop and point of sale systems record transactions, and HR, finance and support tools hold the rest.

slides.title: OLTP vs OLAP
slides.text:
- **OLTP** (operational): many small, fast writes; current state
- **OLAP** (analytical): big reads, aggregations over history

Do not run heavy reports on the production database!
slides.narration: Operational databases are built for many small, fast transactions, called OLTP. Analytics needs huge reads and aggregations over years of history, called OLAP. Running heavy reports directly on production databases can slow down the business, so we copy data to a warehouse.

slides.title: Other sources
slides.text:
- **Event data:** clicks, app usage (product analytics)
- **Files:** spreadsheets, CSV exports
- **APIs** of SaaS tools (ads, payments)
- **External:** market data, weather, public statistics
slides.narration: Beyond operational systems you will find event streams from websites and apps, spreadsheets that teams maintain by hand, APIs from software services like ad platforms and payment providers, and external data such as weather or market statistics.

slides.title: Assess each source
slides.text:
- **Owner** and access rules
- Update **frequency** and latency
- **Grain:** one row = what?
- Keys for joining (customer_id)
- Quality and known issues
slides.narration: For every source, find the owner and access rules, how often it updates, and its grain, meaning what one row represents. Identify the keys that let you join it to other data, and note known quality problems.

slides.title: Ways to extract
slides.text:
- Full extract vs **incremental** (only changes)
- **Change data capture (CDC)** from database logs
- Managed connectors (Fivetran, Airbyte, built-in tool connectors)
- Streaming (Kafka) for real time
slides.narration: Data can be copied in full each time or incrementally, only what changed. Change data capture reads the database log to stream every change. Managed connector services handle hundreds of popular apps, and streaming platforms like Kafka deliver data in near real time.

lessons.notes:
## Typical BI sources

| Source | Examples | Typical data |
|---|---|---|
| ERP | SAP S/4HANA, Oracle, Microsoft Dynamics 365, Odoo | orders, invoices, inventory, GL |
| CRM | Salesforce, HubSpot | leads, accounts, opportunities |
| E-commerce / POS | Shopify, store tills | transactions, baskets |
| Product analytics | app and web events | clicks, sessions, feature use |
| Marketing | ad platforms, email tools | spend, impressions, campaigns |
| Support | ticketing systems | tickets, response times |
| Spreadsheets | budgets, targets, mappings | manual data |
| External | public statistics, weather, FX rates | context data |

## OLTP vs OLAP

| | OLTP | OLAP |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | run the business | analyze the business |
| Queries | many small reads/writes | few large scans and aggregations |
| Data | current state, normalized | history, often denormalized (star schema) |
| Examples | PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server app DBs | Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift, Databricks, Fabric |

## Source inventory

Document each source in a table:

```python
sources = [
    {'name': 'shop_db', 'owner': 'IT', 'grain': 'one row per order line', 'refresh': 'CDC', 'key': 'order_id'},
    {'name': 'targets.xlsx', 'owner': 'Finance', 'grain': 'one row per month per region', 'refresh': 'monthly', 'key': 'month,region'},
]
for s in sources:
    print(f"{s['name']:<13} {s['grain']:<32} {s['refresh']}")
```

## Extraction methods

- **Full load:** simple, but heavy for big tables.
- **Incremental:** use an `updated_at` timestamp or ID watermark.
- **Change data capture (CDC):** read database transaction logs (e.g. Debezium); captures deletes too.
- **APIs:** watch rate limits and pagination.
- **Streaming:** Kafka or cloud equivalents for near real-time dashboards.

## Watch out for

Different IDs for the same customer across systems (needs **master data management**), time zones, currency, soft-deleted records, and spreadsheets that silently change structure.

quiz.q: Which system typically holds leads and sales opportunities?
quiz.explain: CRM systems manage customer relationships and deals.

quiz.q: Why not run heavy BI queries directly on the production OLTP database?
options: They can slow down the live business application
quiz.explain: Analytical scans compete with transactions for resources.

quiz.q: What does the "grain" of a table describe?
quiz.explain: Knowing the grain prevents double counting.

lessons.task:
Create a **source inventory** for an imaginary online bookshop.

For at least five sources write: name, system type (ERP, CRM, events...), owner, grain, refresh frequency, join key, and one known quality risk. Then mark which sources you need for a "monthly revenue by genre and marketing channel" dashboard.

lessons.title: ETL and ELT pipelines
lessons.summary: Extract, transform and load data reliably, and see why modern stacks prefer ELT.

slides.title: Three steps
slides.text:
- **Extract:** copy data out of sources
- **Transform:** clean, join, calculate, aggregate
- **Load:** write into the warehouse
slides.narration: Data pipelines have three steps. Extract copies data out of source systems. Transform cleans it, joins tables, computes new columns and aggregates. Load writes the result into the warehouse.

slides.title: ETL vs ELT
slides.text:
- **ETL:** transform **before** loading (classic, on an ETL server)
- **ELT:** load raw data first, transform **inside** the warehouse with SQL

Cloud warehouses made ELT the default.
slides.narration: In classic ETL, data is transformed on a separate server before loading. In ELT, raw data is loaded first and transformed inside the warehouse using SQL. Powerful cloud warehouses made ELT the modern default because raw data is kept and transformations can be rerun.

slides.title: A tiny ETL in Python
slides.narration: Here is the whole idea in a few lines. We extract rows from CSV text, transform them by cleaning names and computing revenue, and load them into a summary keyed by store.

slides.title: Modern tooling
slides.text:
- Ingestion: Fivetran, Airbyte, built-in connectors
- Transformation: **dbt** (SQL models + tests), Spark
- Orchestration: Airflow, Dagster, Prefect
- Layers: raw -> staging -> marts (bronze, silver, gold)
slides.narration: Modern teams use managed connectors to ingest data, dbt or Spark to transform it with tested SQL or code, and orchestrators like Airflow or Dagster to schedule everything. Data moves through layers, from raw, to cleaned staging, to business-ready marts, sometimes called bronze, silver and gold.

slides.title: Reliable pipelines
slides.text:
- **Idempotent:** rerunning gives the same result
- **Incremental** loads for big tables
- Data **tests** (not null, unique, accepted values)
- Log **rejected rows**; alert on failures
slides.narration: Reliable pipelines are idempotent, so rerunning a job does not double the data. They load incrementally, test data at every layer, log rejected rows instead of silently dropping them, and alert someone when something fails.

lessons.notes:
## ETL vs ELT

| | ETL | ELT |
|---|---|---|
| Where transforms run | separate engine before load | inside the warehouse/lakehouse |
| Raw data kept? | often not | yes (replayable) |
| Typical tools | SSIS, Informatica, Talend | ingestion tool + dbt / SQL / Spark |
| Fits | strict on-prem, sensitive data filtering | cloud warehouses, agility |

## Typical transformations

- Clean: trim text, fix types, standardize codes, handle nulls.
- Deduplicate on business keys.
- Conform: same currency, time zone (UTC), units.
- Join and enrich: add product category, region.
- Derive: `revenue = qty * unit_price`, `month = date[:7]`.
- Aggregate into marts: revenue per month per store.

## Python example: extract, validate, transform, load

```python
import csv, io
raw = 'date,store,qty,price\n2026-01-05, north ,2,5\n2026-01-09,South,x,10\n'
loaded, rejected = {}, 0
for r in csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(raw)):
    try:
        qty, price = int(r['qty']), float(r['price'])
    except ValueError:
        rejected += 1          # log it, do not crash or hide it
        continue
    key = (r['date'][:7], r['store'].strip().title())
    loaded[key] = loaded.get(key, 0) + qty * price
print(loaded, 'rejected', rejected)
```

## dbt in one paragraph

**dbt** lets analytics engineers write transformations as SQL `SELECT` models, organized as staging -> intermediate -> marts, with dependencies, documentation, and tests (`unique`, `not_null`, `relationships`, `accepted_values`) in version control.

```sql
-- models/marts/fct_monthly_revenue.sql
select date_trunc('month', order_date) as month, store, sum(qty * unit_price) as revenue
from {{ ref('stg_orders') }}
group by 1, 2
```

## Pipeline principles

- **Idempotency:** use merges/upserts or partition overwrite, never blind appends.
- **Incremental processing** with watermarks.
- **Slowly changing dimensions (SCD type 2)** to keep history of changing attributes (customer moved region).
- **Observability:** row counts, freshness checks, alerts.
- Version control, code review and CI for pipeline code.

quiz.q: What is the key difference in ELT?
options: Raw data is loaded first and transformed inside the warehouse
quiz.explain: ELT transforms after loading, using warehouse compute.

quiz.q: What does "idempotent" mean for a pipeline?
options: Running it again produces the same result, without duplicates
quiz.explain: Reruns are safe when the pipeline is idempotent.

quiz.q: What should a pipeline do with rows that fail validation?
options: Log or quarantine them and report the count
quiz.explain: Rejected rows must be visible so they can be fixed.

lessons.title: Data warehouses and star schemas
lessons.summary: Model analytical data with fact and dimension tables in a star schema.

slides.title: The data warehouse
slides.text:
A central database **designed for analysis**:
- integrated from many sources
- keeps **history**
- optimized for big reads (columnar storage)

Cloud: Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift, Databricks, Fabric
slides.narration: A data warehouse is a central database designed for analysis. It integrates data from many sources, keeps history, and stores data in columns so huge aggregations run fast. Popular cloud options include Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift, Databricks and Microsoft Fabric.

slides.title: Facts and dimensions
slides.text:
- **Fact table:** events / measurements (sales lines): numbers + foreign keys
- **Dimension tables:** context (who, what, where, when): product, customer, store, date
slides.narration: Dimensional modeling splits data into facts and dimensions. A fact table records events, like each sales line, with numeric measures and keys. Dimension tables describe the context: which product, which customer, which store, and which date.

slides.title: The star schema
slides.text:
```
        dim_date
           |
dim_product - fact_sales - dim_store
           |
       dim_customer
```
One fact in the middle, dimensions around it.
slides.narration: Draw the fact table in the middle and the dimensions around it, and you get a star, hence the name star schema. Queries join the fact to the dimensions they need, then group and sum. BI tools are designed to work best with this shape.

slides.title: Grain first
slides.text:
Declare the **grain**: "one row per order line".

All facts must match the grain, or sums double count.
slides.narration: The first design decision is the grain, what exactly one fact row represents, for example one row per order line. Every measure in the fact table must match that grain, otherwise totals will be double counted.

slides.title: Joining fact to dimension
slides.narration: In code, joining a fact to a dimension is just a lookup by key. Here each sale finds its product's category, and we sum revenue by category, exactly what a BI tool does behind the scenes.

slides.title: Snowflake schema and more
slides.text:
- **Snowflake schema:** dimensions normalized into sub-tables
- **Surrogate keys**, **SCD type 2** for history
- **Conformed dimensions** shared across facts
- Lakehouse: open table formats (Delta, Iceberg)
slides.narration: A snowflake schema normalizes dimensions into extra tables, saving space at the cost of more joins. Warehouses use surrogate keys and slowly changing dimensions to keep history, share conformed dimensions across fact tables, and lakehouses store tables in open formats like Delta and Iceberg.

lessons.notes:
## Why a warehouse?

Operational databases are normalized for fast transactions. A **data warehouse** is organized for **analysis**: integrated, historical, consistent, and fast for aggregations (columnar storage, massively parallel processing). A **lakehouse** combines cheap object storage with warehouse features using open table formats (Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg).

## Dimensional modeling (Kimball)

Four steps:
1. Choose the **business process** (sales, shipments, support tickets).
2. Declare the **grain** (one row per order line).
3. Identify the **dimensions** (date, product, customer, store, channel).
4. Identify the **facts** (quantity, amount, discount).

## Fact tables

- Numeric, additive measures (`qty`, `amount`) plus foreign keys to dimensions.
- Types: **transaction** (one row per event), **periodic snapshot** (stock per day), **accumulating snapshot** (order pipeline stages).
- Beware non-additive measures (ratios, distinct counts): store the parts and compute later.

## Dimension tables

- Descriptive attributes used to filter and group: `product_name`, `category`, `brand`.
- **Surrogate keys** (integers) instead of source IDs.
- **Date dimension** with year, quarter, month, weekday, holiday flags.
- **Slowly changing dimensions:** type 1 overwrite, type 2 add a new row with valid-from/valid-to to keep history.

## A star schema query

```sql
SELECT d.year, p.category, SUM(f.amount) AS revenue
FROM fact_sales f
JOIN dim_date d    ON f.date_key = d.date_key
JOIN dim_product p ON f.product_key = p.product_key
WHERE d.year = 2026
GROUP BY d.year, p.category
ORDER BY revenue DESC;
```

## Star vs snowflake

| | Star | Snowflake |
|---|---|---|
| Dimensions | denormalized, wide | normalized into sub-tables |
| Joins | fewer, simpler | more |
| BI tool friendliness | best | ok |

Power BI, Tableau and Looker all perform best on star schemas. Keep facts long and narrow, dimensions wide and short.

## Data marts

A **data mart** is a subject-specific subset (finance mart, marketing mart), often a set of stars sharing **conformed dimensions** such as date and customer.

quiz.q: What does a fact table mainly contain?
options: Numeric measures and keys to dimensions
quiz.explain: Facts store measurable events.

quiz.q: Which table answers "which category does this product belong to?"
quiz.explain: Descriptive attributes live in dimensions.

quiz.q: Why declare the grain first?
options: So every measure matches what one row means and nothing is double counted
quiz.explain: Mixed grains cause wrong totals.

lessons.title: OLAP: slicing, dicing and cubes
lessons.summary: Analyze data across dimensions with roll-up, drill-down, slice, dice and pivot.

slides.title: Thinking in cubes
slides.text:
An **OLAP cube**: measures (revenue) at the intersection of dimensions (product x region x time).

Every cell = an aggregate.
slides.narration: OLAP stands for online analytical processing. Picture your data as a cube with one dimension along each edge, such as product, region and time. Each cell holds an aggregated measure, like revenue for one product, in one region, in one month.

slides.title: The operations
slides.text:
- **Roll-up:** month -> quarter -> year (less detail)
- **Drill-down:** year -> quarter -> month (more detail)
- **Slice:** fix one dimension (only 2026)
- **Dice:** filter several (2026, Europe, Books)
- **Pivot:** swap rows and columns
slides.narration: There are five classic operations. Roll up to see less detail, like years instead of months. Drill down for more detail. Slice by fixing one dimension, dice by filtering several, and pivot by swapping what appears in rows and columns.

slides.title: A pivot in code
slides.narration: A pivot table is a two-dimensional view of the cube. In plain Python a dictionary keyed by region and quarter does the job, and missing combinations become zero.

slides.title: Hierarchies
slides.text:
Dimensions have levels:
- Date: year > quarter > month > day
- Geography: country > region > city > store
- Product: category > subcategory > product
slides.narration: Dimensions usually have hierarchies. Dates go from year to quarter to month to day. Geography goes from country to city to store. Drill down and roll up move along these hierarchies.

slides.title: OLAP today
slides.text:
- Classic: MOLAP cubes (SSAS)
- Modern: columnar warehouses compute on the fly (ROLAP)
- In-memory models: Power BI semantic models, Tableau extracts
- SQL: GROUP BY ROLLUP / CUBE / GROUPING SETS
slides.narration: Classic OLAP pre-computed cubes in special servers. Today, fast columnar warehouses compute aggregates on the fly, while tools like Power BI keep compressed in-memory models. SQL itself supports rollup and cube to compute subtotals.

lessons.notes:
## The cube model

OLAP (Online Analytical Processing) organizes data by **dimensions** (product, region, time, channel) and **measures** (revenue, units, margin). A cube is conceptual: in practice it can be a star schema queried by a fast engine.

## Operations

| Operation | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Roll-up | aggregate up a hierarchy | months -> quarters |
| Drill-down | go to finer detail | country -> city |
| Slice | fix one dimension to one value | year = 2026 |
| Dice | select a sub-cube with several filters | 2026, EU, Books+Games |
| Pivot | rotate the view | regions as columns |
| Drill-through | see the underlying rows | the orders behind a cell |

## SQL for OLAP

```sql
-- subtotals per region and a grand total
SELECT region, quarter, SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM sales
GROUP BY ROLLUP (region, quarter);

-- all combinations of subtotals
SELECT region, channel, SUM(amount) FROM sales GROUP BY CUBE (region, channel);
```

## A pivot with totals in Python

```python
rows = [('North', 'Q1', 100), ('North', 'Q2', 120), ('South', 'Q1', 80)]
regions = sorted({r for r, _, _ in rows})
quarters = sorted({q for _, q, _ in rows})
cell = {}
for r, q, a in rows:
    cell[(r, q)] = cell.get((r, q), 0) + a
print('region', *quarters, 'total')
for r in regions:
    vals = [cell.get((r, q), 0) for q in quarters]
    print(r, *vals, sum(vals))
```

## Types of OLAP engines

- **MOLAP:** pre-aggregated multidimensional storage (classic SQL Server Analysis Services). Very fast, less flexible.
- **ROLAP:** queries a relational warehouse directly.
- **HOLAP:** mixes both.
- Modern: columnar cloud warehouses and in-memory engines (Power BI VertiPaq, DuckDB, ClickHouse) make most aggregations interactive without pre-built cubes.

## Additivity

- **Additive** measures (revenue) sum across all dimensions.
- **Semi-additive** (account balance, stock level) sum across products but not across time; use the last value per period.
- **Non-additive** (ratios, distinct counts) must be recomputed from components at each level.

quiz.q: Going from monthly to yearly totals is called...
quiz.explain: Roll-up aggregates to a higher level.

quiz.q: Filtering the cube to only year 2026 is a...
quiz.explain: A slice fixes one dimension value.

quiz.q: Why can't you sum stock levels across months?
options: Stock is semi-additive: summing over time double counts
quiz.explain: Use the period-end value instead.

lessons.title: SQL for BI
lessons.summary: Write the SQL patterns BI work relies on: aggregates, joins, CASE, date grouping and window functions.

slides.title: SQL is the language of BI
slides.text:
Every warehouse and BI tool speaks SQL.

Core pattern:
**SELECT** dims, **AGG**(measure)
**FROM** fact **JOIN** dims
**WHERE** filters **GROUP BY** dims
slides.narration: SQL is the shared language of BI. Every warehouse and every BI tool uses it, even when you only drag and drop. Almost every report is the same pattern: select some dimensions and aggregated measures, join, filter, and group.

slides.title: Aggregates and HAVING
slides.text:
- COUNT(*), COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id)
- SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX
- **WHERE** filters rows before grouping
- **HAVING** filters groups after
slides.narration: The aggregate functions count, sum, average, minimum and maximum summarize groups. Count distinct counts unique customers. Remember the order: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping, HAVING filters whole groups afterwards.

slides.title: SQLite from Python
slides.text: Python ships with **sqlite3**, a real SQL database:
slides.code:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE sales(region TEXT, amount REAL)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO sales VALUES (?, ?)",
               [("North", 100), ("South", 80), ("North", 50)])
q = "SELECT region, SUM(amount) FROM sales GROUP BY region ORDER BY 2 DESC"
for row in db.execute(q):
    print(row)
slides.narration: You can practise SQL right here, because Python includes SQLite in its standard library. We create an in-memory database, insert rows and run a GROUP BY query.

slides.title: CASE and dates
slides.text:
- **CASE WHEN** for buckets: order size, segments
- Group by month: date_trunc('month', d) or strftime('%Y-%m', d) in SQLite
- Conditional sums: SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'refund' THEN amount END)
slides.narration: CASE expressions create categories on the fly, like small, medium and large orders, and enable conditional sums. To group by month, truncate dates: most warehouses use date trunc, while SQLite uses strftime.

slides.title: Window functions
slides.text:
Calculate across rows **without collapsing** them:
- running totals: SUM(x) OVER (ORDER BY month)
- rank: RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY revenue DESC)
- previous period: LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month)
slides.narration: Window functions are a BI superpower. They compute across related rows while keeping each row. Use them for running totals, rankings within each region, and comparing a month with the previous one using LAG.

lessons.notes:
## The BI query skeleton

```sql
SELECT   p.category,
         strftime('%Y-%m', f.order_date) AS month,     -- date_trunc('month', ...) in most warehouses
         COUNT(DISTINCT f.customer_id)   AS customers,
         SUM(f.amount)                   AS revenue
FROM     fact_sales f
JOIN     dim_product p ON p.product_id = f.product_id
WHERE    f.status = 'completed'
GROUP BY p.category, month
HAVING   SUM(f.amount) > 1000
ORDER BY revenue DESC;
```

Logical order of execution: FROM/JOIN -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> SELECT -> ORDER BY -> LIMIT.

## Joins

- `INNER JOIN`: only matching rows.
- `LEFT JOIN`: keep all rows from the left (facts), even without a match; check for NULLs.
- Watch out for **fan-out**: joining to a table with several rows per key multiplies your sums.

## CASE expressions

```sql
SELECT CASE WHEN amount >= 100 THEN 'large'
            WHEN amount >= 20  THEN 'medium'
            ELSE 'small' END AS size,
       COUNT(*) AS orders
FROM orders GROUP BY size;
```

## Window functions

```sql
SELECT month, revenue,
       SUM(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month)                     AS running_total,
       revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month)           AS change_vs_prev,
       RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY revenue DESC) AS rank_in_region
FROM monthly_revenue;
```

## CTEs for readability

```sql
WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', order_date) AS month, SUM(amount) AS revenue
  FROM orders GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT month, revenue, revenue * 100.0 / (SELECT SUM(revenue) FROM monthly) AS pct
FROM monthly;
```

## Practising with sqlite3

Python's `sqlite3` module gives you a full SQL engine with no installation, including window functions (SQLite 3.25+). Warehouses (BigQuery, Snowflake, Postgres) differ mainly in date functions and some syntax.

## Good habits

Name columns clearly, comment business logic, test totals against a trusted source, avoid `SELECT *` on large tables, and filter early to reduce scanned data (and cost).

quiz.q: Which clause filters groups after aggregation?
quiz.explain: HAVING applies to grouped results.

quiz.q: Which expression counts unique customers?
quiz.explain: DISTINCT removes duplicates before counting.

quiz.q: What does LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) return?
options: The previous row's revenue in month order
quiz.explain: LAG looks back one row in the window order.

exercise.solution:
import sqlite3
n = int(input())
rows = []
for _ in range(n):
    oid, cust, region, amount, status = input().split()
    rows.append((int(oid), cust, region, float(amount), status))
db = sqlite3.connect(':memory:')
db.execute('CREATE TABLE orders(id INTEGER, customer TEXT, region TEXT, amount REAL, status TEXT)')
db.executemany('INSERT INTO orders VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)', rows)
query = """
SELECT region,
       COUNT(*) AS orders,
       COUNT(DISTINCT customer) AS customers,
       SUM(amount) AS revenue,
       AVG(amount) AS avg_order
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'completed'
GROUP BY region
HAVING SUM(amount) >= 100
ORDER BY revenue DESC, region
"""
result = db.execute(query).fetchall()
if not result:
    print('no data')
for region, orders, customers, revenue, avg in result:
    print(f'{region} {orders} {customers} {revenue:.2f} {avg:.2f}')

lessons.title: Dashboards and reports
lessons.summary: Design dashboards that people actually use: audience, layout, KPIs, filters and performance.

slides.title: Dashboard vs report
slides.text:
- **Dashboard:** at-a-glance monitoring, interactive, few KPIs, refreshed often
- **Report:** detailed, often paginated/printable, scheduled (monthly finance pack)
- **Ad hoc analysis:** one question, one time
slides.narration: A dashboard gives an at-a-glance view of a few key numbers and is interactive and frequently refreshed. A report is more detailed, often paginated and sent on a schedule. Ad hoc analysis answers a one-off question.

slides.title: Start with the user
slides.text:
Ask:
- Who uses it, how often, on what device?
- Which **decisions** will it support?
- Which 3-7 **KPIs** answer those?

Sketch on paper before building.
slides.narration: Start with the user, not the tool. Who will use the dashboard, how often, and on what device? Which decisions should it support, and which handful of KPIs answer those decisions? Sketch it on paper before you open any software.

slides.title: Layout
slides.text:
- Top-left: most important KPIs (cards with vs target / vs last period)
- Then trends (line charts), then breakdowns (bars)
- Details and tables at the bottom
- Consistent colours; filters at the top
slides.narration: People read from the top left, so put the most important KPI cards there, each compared with target or the previous period. Below come trends, then breakdowns by region or product, and finally detailed tables. Keep filters at the top and colours consistent.

slides.title: Common mistakes
slides.text:
- 25 charts on one page
- KPIs with no comparison ("revenue 92k", good or bad?)
- Pie charts with 12 slices, 3D effects
- Slow loading (over ~5 seconds)
- No definition of metrics
slides.narration: Common mistakes include cramming twenty five charts on a page, showing numbers with no comparison so nobody knows whether they are good, pies with too many slices, slow loading, and no explanation of how metrics are defined.

slides.title: Keep it alive
slides.text:
- Show **data freshness** ("updated 08:00")
- Add metric definitions / tooltips
- Track **usage**; retire unused dashboards
- Alerts and subscriptions for thresholds
slides.narration: A dashboard is a product. Show when data was last refreshed, explain metrics in tooltips, check usage statistics and retire dashboards nobody opens. Set up alerts and email subscriptions so important changes reach people automatically.

lessons.notes:
## Types of BI output

| Type | Purpose | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Strategic dashboard | leadership monitors goals | company KPIs, monthly |
| Operational dashboard | real-time monitoring | warehouse orders today |
| Analytical dashboard | explore drivers | sales by segment with drill-down |
| Paginated report | detailed, printable, regulatory | invoice lists, finance packs |
| Alerts / subscriptions | push information | "stock below 100 units" |

## Design process

1. **Interview users:** goals, decisions, questions, frequency, device.
2. **Choose KPIs** with clear definitions and targets.
3. **Wireframe** on paper or a whiteboard.
4. **Build** on a clean, modeled dataset (star schema / semantic model).
5. **Test** with users; check numbers against trusted sources.
6. **Launch, train, measure usage, iterate.**

## Layout guidelines

- **Z-pattern:** top-left KPI cards -> top-right -> trends -> details.
- Each KPI card: value, comparison (vs target, vs previous period), small sparkline, colour only for status.
- 5 to 9 visuals per page is plenty; use drill-through pages for detail.
- Consistent number formats (k, M), units and date ranges.
- Accessibility: contrast, colour-blind-safe palettes, alt text.

## KPI card logic

```python
def card(name, value, target, prev):
    vs_target = value / target * 100
    vs_prev = (value - prev) / prev * 100
    status = 'green' if vs_target >= 100 else 'amber' if vs_target >= 90 else 'red'
    return f'{name}: {value:,.0f} ({vs_target:.0f}% of target, {vs_prev:+.1f}% vs prev) [{status}]'
print(card('Revenue', 92000, 100000, 80000))
```

## Performance

- Pre-aggregate heavy data; use import/extract modes or aggregations.
- Limit visuals and high-cardinality filters per page.
- Push filters to the source; avoid complex row-by-row calculations.

## Trust

Show the **last refresh time**, link a **metric glossary**, and certify official dashboards so users know which ones are the source of truth.

quiz.q: What should almost every KPI card include?
options: A comparison such as vs target or vs previous period
quiz.explain: Without context, a number cannot be judged.

quiz.q: Where should the most important KPIs go?
quiz.explain: Readers scan from the top left first.

quiz.q: What is a paginated report best for?
quiz.explain: Paginated reports format detailed data for printing or PDF.

lessons.task:
Design a **sales manager dashboard** on paper or in a drawing tool.

1. Write the user, the 3 decisions it supports, and refresh frequency.
2. Choose 4 to 6 KPIs with definitions and comparisons.
3. Sketch the layout: KPI cards, one trend chart, two breakdown charts, one detail table, and filters.
4. Add where you will show data freshness and metric definitions.
5. List one alert that should be sent automatically.

lessons.title: BI tools: Power BI, Tableau, Looker, Metabase
lessons.summary: Compare the leading BI tools and the features that matter when choosing one.

slides.title: Microsoft Power BI
slides.text:
- Market leader, part of **Microsoft Fabric**
- Power Query (data prep), **DAX** (measures)
- Desktop app (Windows) + web service
- Strong with Excel, Teams, Azure
slides.code:
Total Revenue = SUM(Sales[Amount])
Revenue LY = CALCULATE([Total Revenue],
    SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR('Date'[Date]))
YoY % = DIVIDE([Total Revenue] - [Revenue LY], [Revenue LY])
slides.narration: Power BI from Microsoft is the most widely used BI tool. It is part of the Microsoft Fabric platform, uses Power Query to prepare data and the DAX language for measures, and fits naturally into organizations that live in Excel, Teams and Azure.

slides.title: Tableau
slides.text:
- Known for **visual exploration** and beautiful charts
- Drag-and-drop "VizQL"
- Tableau Desktop, Cloud, Server
- Owned by **Salesforce**; AI features built in
slides.narration: Tableau, owned by Salesforce, is famous for fast visual exploration. You drag fields onto shelves and it draws the chart. Analysts love its flexibility, and it is available as a desktop app, in the cloud or on your own servers.

slides.title: Looker
slides.text:
- **Google Cloud**
- **LookML:** a code-based **semantic layer** defining metrics once
- Version-controlled with Git
- Not the same as free **Looker Studio**
slides.narration: Looker, part of Google Cloud, is built around LookML, a modeling language where metrics and joins are defined once in code and version controlled with Git. Do not confuse it with Looker Studio, Google's free, simpler reporting tool.

slides.title: Metabase and open source
slides.text:
- **Metabase:** open source, simple "questions", easy self-hosting
- **Apache Superset:** open source, SQL-centric
- Others: Qlik, ThoughtSpot, Sigma, Mode
slides.narration: Metabase is an open source tool that is very quick to set up, letting people ask simple questions without SQL. Apache Superset is another open source option. Other notable tools include Qlik, ThoughtSpot and Sigma.

slides.title: How to choose
slides.text:
- Existing ecosystem (Microsoft, Google, Salesforce)
- Users: self-service vs analysts
- **Semantic layer** and governance
- Cost (per user / capacity), hosting, security
- AI assistants on governed data

Run a **proof of concept** with real data.
slides.narration: Choose based on your ecosystem, your users, governance and semantic layer needs, pricing and hosting. All major tools now include AI assistants, which only answer well on clean, governed models. Always test a short proof of concept with your real data.

lessons.notes:
## The landscape (2026)

| Tool | Vendor | Strengths | Modeling language |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Power BI** | Microsoft (Fabric) | price/value, Excel & Microsoft 365 integration, huge community | Power Query (M), **DAX** |
| **Tableau** | Salesforce | visual exploration, design flexibility | calculated fields, LOD expressions |
| **Looker** | Google Cloud | governed semantic layer, Git workflow, embedding | **LookML** |
| **Looker Studio** | Google | free, simple reports | — |
| **Metabase** | open source / cloud | quick setup, simple questions, self-hosting | SQL + GUI |
| **Apache Superset** | open source | SQL-centric, scalable | SQL |
| Qlik, ThoughtSpot, Sigma | various | associative engine, search-driven, spreadsheet-like | various |

## Key concepts per tool

**Power BI:** build a **semantic model** (star schema) with relationships, write **measures** in DAX, publish to the service, share via workspaces and apps, secure with row-level security (RLS).

```
Margin % = DIVIDE(SUM(Sales[Profit]), SUM(Sales[Revenue]))
```

**Tableau:** connect live or via extracts; dimensions vs measures; **LOD expressions** such as `{FIXED [Customer] : MIN([Order Date])}` for first purchase date.

**Looker:** LookML defines views, dimensions, measures and explores once; every dashboard reuses the same definitions.

```
measure: total_revenue {
  type: sum
  sql: ${TABLE}.amount ;;
}
```

**Metabase:** point it at a database, ask "questions" through a GUI or SQL, build dashboards, set alerts.

## Selection criteria

1. Data sources and warehouse compatibility.
2. Semantic layer and governance (certified datasets, lineage, RLS).
3. Self-service ease for business users vs depth for analysts.
4. Sharing, embedding, mobile, alerting.
5. AI features (natural-language Q&A, summaries) and how they respect permissions.
6. Licensing model and total cost of ownership; cloud vs self-hosted.
7. Skills already in the team.

## Universal skills

Whatever the tool: star schemas, clear metric definitions, SQL, good chart design, and governance transfer directly. Tools change; these skills do not.

quiz.q: Which language defines measures in Power BI?
quiz.explain: DAX (Data Analysis Expressions) is used for Power BI measures.

quiz.q: What is LookML?
quiz.explain: LookML defines dimensions, measures and joins once.

quiz.q: Which tool is open source and quick to self-host?
quiz.explain: Metabase has an open source edition that is easy to self-host.

lessons.task:
Compare two BI tools for a 50-person company that uses Microsoft 365 and a PostgreSQL database.

1. Make a table with 6 criteria (cost, ease of use, data connection, sharing, governance, AI features).
2. Score each tool 1 to 5 and justify each score in one sentence (use the vendors' current documentation and pricing pages).
3. Recommend one tool and describe a two-week proof of concept: which dashboard, which users, and which success criteria.

lessons.title: Data governance and quality
lessons.summary: Make BI trustworthy with ownership, definitions, security and automated data quality checks.

slides.title: Why governance?
slides.text:
Without it:
- 3 dashboards, 3 revenue numbers
- nobody knows who owns a table
- sensitive data visible to everyone

Governance = **rules, roles and processes** for data.
slides.narration: Without governance, every team defines revenue differently, nobody knows who owns which table, and sensitive data leaks to people who should not see it. Data governance sets the rules, roles and processes that keep data trustworthy and safe.

slides.title: Roles
slides.text:
- **Data owner:** accountable for a domain (Head of Sales)
- **Data steward:** maintains definitions and quality
- **Data custodian:** IT team operating the systems
- Data governance council for decisions
slides.narration: Governance assigns clear roles. A data owner is accountable for a business domain, a data steward maintains definitions and quality day to day, and a custodian, usually IT, runs the systems. A small council resolves conflicts and approves standards.

slides.title: Dimensions of data quality
slides.text:
- **Completeness:** no missing values where required
- **Validity:** follows rules/formats
- **Uniqueness:** no duplicates
- **Consistency** across systems
- **Accuracy**, **timeliness**
slides.narration: Data quality has several dimensions. Completeness means required values are present. Validity means values follow the rules. Uniqueness means no duplicates. Consistency means systems agree. Accuracy and timeliness mean data is correct and fresh enough.

slides.title: Automate the checks
slides.text: Write tests that run with every load:
slides.code:
rows = [("1", "a@x.com"), ("2", ""), ("2", "b@x")]
ids = [r[0] for r in rows]
dupes = len(ids) - len(set(ids))
missing = sum(1 for _, e in rows if not e)
print("duplicates", dupes, "missing emails", missing)
slides.narration: Quality should be checked automatically every time data loads. Simple rules, like no duplicate IDs and valid email formats, catch most problems before anyone sees a wrong dashboard.

slides.title: Security and compliance
slides.text:
- **Least privilege**, role-based access
- **Row-level security** (managers see their region)
- Mask PII; data classification
- GDPR/CCPA: purpose, retention, deletion
- **Catalog** and **lineage**
slides.narration: Protect data with least privilege and role-based access. Row-level security shows each manager only their region. Classify and mask personal data, follow laws like GDPR on purpose and retention, and keep a data catalog with lineage so people know where every number comes from.

lessons.notes:
## Data governance

The framework of **people, processes and technology** that ensures data is accurate, secure, documented and used appropriately.

Building blocks:
- **Ownership and stewardship** for each data domain.
- **Business glossary / metric definitions** (one definition of "active customer").
- **Data catalog** (e.g. Microsoft Purview, Unity Catalog, Collibra, Alation, DataHub, OpenMetadata) with descriptions, owners, and **lineage** from source to dashboard.
- **Access policies**: role-based access control, row-level and column-level security, masking of personal data.
- **Compliance**: GDPR, CCPA, sector rules; retention and deletion policies; audit logs.

## Data quality dimensions

| Dimension | Example check |
|---|---|
| Completeness | email is not null |
| Validity | age between 0 and 120; country in ISO list |
| Uniqueness | customer_id unique |
| Consistency | order total = sum of lines; CRM and ERP agree |
| Accuracy | matches the real world / trusted source |
| Timeliness | table refreshed within the last 24 hours |

## Automated checks

Tools: dbt tests, Great Expectations, Soda, warehouse-native data quality features, and data observability platforms that detect anomalies in volume, freshness and schema.

```python
allowed = {'PT', 'ES', 'FR'}
rows = [('1', 'a@x.com', '30', 'PT'), ('1', 'bad', '200', 'XX')]
seen, issues = set(), 0
for rid, email, age, country in rows:
    bad = rid in seen or '@' not in email or not (age.isdigit() and int(age) <= 120) or country not in allowed
    seen.add(rid)
    issues += bad
print(f'quality score {(len(rows) - issues) / len(rows):.0%}')
```

## Data contracts

A **data contract** is an agreement between data producers (app teams) and consumers (BI) on schema, meaning and quality, enforced in CI so breaking changes are caught before they reach dashboards.

## Process

1. Profile data to find issues.
2. Define rules with business owners.
3. Automate checks in pipelines; block or quarantine bad data.
4. Alert owners; track a **data quality score** over time.
5. Fix at the **source**, not only in the warehouse.

Governance should enable people, not block them: certify trusted datasets so self-service users build on solid ground.

quiz.q: Who is accountable for a data domain such as sales data?
quiz.explain: Owners are accountable; stewards maintain day to day.

quiz.q: Two rows share customer_id 42. Which quality dimension fails?
quiz.explain: IDs must be unique.

quiz.q: What does row-level security do?
options: Restricts which rows each user can see
quiz.explain: For example, a manager only sees their own region.

lessons.title: A BI project from start to finish
lessons.summary: Run a complete BI project: requirements, data, model, dashboard, launch and continuous improvement.

slides.title: Phase 1: Discover
slides.text:
- Stakeholders and their **decisions**
- Business questions and KPIs
- Success criteria ("weekly review uses the dashboard")
- Scope: what is **out**
slides.narration: Every BI project starts with discovery. Meet the stakeholders, learn which decisions they make, turn their questions into KPIs, agree how success will be measured, and write down what is out of scope.

slides.title: Phase 2: Data
slides.text:
- Inventory sources, owners, access
- Profile data quality
- Agree **metric definitions** with owners
- Build pipelines (ELT) and tests
slides.narration: Next, find and understand the data. List the sources and owners, get access, profile quality, and agree on precise metric definitions with the business owners. Then build the pipelines with tests.

slides.title: Phase 3: Model and build
slides.text:
- Star schema: facts + dimensions
- Semantic layer / measures
- Wireframe -> prototype dashboard
- Validate numbers against finance or source reports
slides.narration: Then model the data as a star schema, define measures in a semantic layer, wireframe the dashboard and build a prototype. Before anyone sees it, reconcile the numbers against trusted sources like finance reports.

slides.title: Phase 4: Launch and adopt
slides.text:
- User acceptance testing (UAT)
- Security (row-level), documentation
- Training, office hours
- Announce; retire old spreadsheets
slides.narration: Launching is more than publishing. Run user acceptance testing, set up security, write documentation, train users, and retire the old spreadsheets so everyone moves to the new single source of truth.

slides.title: Phase 5: Operate and improve
slides.text:
- Monitor refresh failures, quality, usage
- Collect feedback; backlog of improvements
- Version control and change process
- Measure **business impact**
slides.narration: Finally, operate and improve. Monitor refreshes, data quality and usage, keep a backlog of feedback, manage changes through version control, and measure whether the dashboard really improved decisions.

lessons.notes:
## A project plan template

| Phase | Key outputs |
|---|---|
| 1. Discover | stakeholder map, business questions, KPI list, success criteria, scope |
| 2. Data | source inventory, access, data profiling, metric definitions, ELT pipelines with tests |
| 3. Model | star schema, semantic model/measures, documentation |
| 4. Build | wireframes, prototype, final dashboard and reports |
| 5. Validate | reconciliation with trusted numbers, user acceptance testing (UAT) |
| 6. Launch | security (RLS), training, communication, retire old reports |
| 7. Operate | monitoring, support, usage tracking, iteration |

## Example: retail sales dashboard

- **Question:** "Which stores and categories are behind target this month, and why?"
- **KPIs:** revenue vs target, gross margin %, average basket, conversion (footfall to sales), stock-outs.
- **Sources:** POS database (CDC), product master (ERP), targets (finance spreadsheet), footfall counters (API).
- **Model:** `fact_sales` (grain: receipt line), `fact_targets` (store-month), dimensions date, store, product.
- **Dashboard:** KPI cards, revenue trend vs target, store ranking, category breakdown, drill-through to products.
- **Governance:** store managers see only their store (RLS); data refresh daily at 06:00 with freshness check.

## Reconciliation check

```python
warehouse_total = 1_254_300.50
finance_total = 1_254_812.00
diff_pct = abs(warehouse_total - finance_total) / finance_total * 100
print(f'difference {diff_pct:.3f}%', 'OK' if diff_pct < 0.1 else 'INVESTIGATE')
```

Agree tolerances in advance and explain known differences (timing, refunds, currency).

## Working agile

Deliver in small increments: one KPI end to end first, then expand. Show a working prototype in week two rather than a perfect dashboard in month three.

## Risks and how to handle them

- **Unclear definitions:** get sign-off from metric owners.
- **Poor source data:** report issues to source owners; show data quality on the dashboard.
- **Low adoption:** involve users early, train them, embed the dashboard in meetings.
- **Scope creep:** maintain a backlog and prioritize by business value.

## Career tip

Document your project as a case study: problem, data, model, dashboard screenshots, impact. It is the best portfolio piece for BI roles.

quiz.q: What should come first in a BI project?
quiz.explain: Discovery defines what the project must deliver.

quiz.q: Why reconcile dashboard numbers with finance reports before launch?
options: To catch errors and build trust
quiz.explain: Matching trusted numbers proves the pipeline is right.

quiz.q: What is a good way to reduce risk of low adoption?
options: Involve users early and train them
Hide the old reports without notice
quiz.explain: Engaged, trained users adopt new tools.
